correctness.rationale: For each vertex and colour the count among open neighbours is at most half the vertex degree. With two colours the part sign-sum equations force every part to be even; the converse is immediate. Four colours are necessary for \(K_4\) and \(K_{1,1,2}\). A two-different-colour twin-pair augmentation preserves every strong-majority inequality. After reduction of each part to one or two vertices, constructive three-colour patterns cover all nonexceptional residual cores; exceptional four-vertex cores extended by any available pair become one of three explicitly coloured six-vertex cores. Exhaustive direct checking for 51 unordered part-size profiles up to eight vertices and constructive checking of 9,246 profiles through 25 vertices supplement, but do not replace, the unrestricted proof.

evidence: Kalinowski et al. prove a general upper bound \(\operatorname{Maj}(G)\le2\Delta(G)+1\) and give the \(K_4\) exception; their theorem allows values far larger than three.
Chawda et al. treat adversarial majority colouring games; a game threshold does not give an exact value of the static invariant in an arbitrary multipartite graph.
broader_coverage.reasoning: The degree-dependent broad bound is weaker than the three-colour classification for growing complete multipartite graphs. The known complete-graph case covers \(K_4\) alone but cannot establish the new noncomplete \(K_{1,1,2}\) obstruction or all other sizes. Game and edge parameters are distinct.

Kalinowski et al. imply Maj(\(K_4\))=4, and their general 2Δ+1 bound does not imply the sharp multipartite bound.

claim_vs_prior_implication.reasoning: The original portion is a sharp upper bound of three outside two precise four-vertex exceptions and a constructive method. The strongest inspected prior claims neither contain that upper bound nor supply a general implication by parameter domination; the known binary and \(K_4\) statements are expressly excluded from novelty.

evidence: Strong majority: every open-neighbourhood colour count is at most half the degree (Kalinowski et al., §1).
Neighbourhood-balanced binary colouring forces exact half counts in every neighbourhood (Freyberg–Marr, Theorem 4).
The multiple-colour neighbourhood lambda-balance predicate in Collins et al. fixes a distinct target neighbourhood balance, not the present minimum palette problem.
equivalent_formulations.reasoning: Binary strong-majority and two-colour neighbourhood balance are logically equivalent, so the even-part criterion is preexisting. Neither exact two-colour balancing nor fixed-ratio neighbourhood-balance claims determine whether three colours suffice with the per-colour upper-half constraint. Static vertex colouring is not edge strong-majority colouring or the adversarial majority game.

originality.rationale: The already-published two-colour parity criterion (Freyberg–Marr 2024, Theorem 4) and the \(K_4\) obstruction (Kalinowski et al. 2026) are explicitly credited rather than claimed. The new exact three-versus-four outcome for complete multipartite graphs, particularly the additional \(K_{1,1,2}\) obstruction and the universal twin-pair construction, is not implied by those statements. Full primary-text comparison with Kalinowski et al. (2026), Freyberg and Marr (2024), Collins et al. (2026), and Chawda et al. (2026), plus targeted mathematical-record and literature queries, found no covering theorem. Residual risk remains from alternative terminology and unindexed literature; absence in search is not a proof of universal novelty.
residual_risks: Equivalent exact three-colour bounds may exist in unindexed literature under static neighborhood-majority terminology.

value.rationale: This determines a natural, recently introduced static graph invariant on an infinite family of arbitrarily high degree, replacing a degree-dependent bound with a sharp three-colour threshold and exactly two explicit four-colour exceptions. The pair-extension lemma provides a reusable constructive mechanism; the noncomplete four-colour obstruction cannot be inferred from the already-known \(K_4\) result. The novelty claim excludes the known binary criterion and ordinary exact computations.
